claims.text: Mechanical alloying for 5–6 hours under inert atmosphere followed by vacuum SPS at 900 °C for 10 minutes is the proposed processing route.
The as-blended Mg–Ti/Zr/Hf/Nb powders are prone to elemental segregation and multiphase formation during heating.
Mechanical alloying will produce a nanocrystalline solid solution with grain size below 50 nm in the Mg-transition-metal alloy.
Mechanical alloying will generate a high dislocation density in the Mg-transition-metal alloy.
The nanocrystalline grain structure and high dislocation density lower the activation energy for solid-solution formation.
Mechanical alloying kinetically traps the Mg alloy in a metastable single-phase state before segregation can occur.
Mechanical alloying creates a supersaturated solid solution with reduced lattice distortion.
Vacuum SPS at 900 °C, a heating rate of 50 °C/min, and a 10-minute hold are established processing parameters for a mechanically alloyed transition-metal alloy.
Applying 50 MPa during SPS is an applicable condition for the proposed 900 °C Mg-alloy process.
Rapid heating and a short SPS dwell at 900 °C cause rapid densification through interface-controlled growth with an Avrami exponent of approximately 2.
SPS at 900 °C for 10 minutes provides insufficient time and thermal energy for brittle Laves phases to nucleate.
The rapid 900 °C SPS cycle prevents Mg segregation and volatilization.
The proposed route will produce greater than 95% relative density.
The proposed route will produce a single-phase-like BCC or FCC microstructure with significantly reduced elemental segregation.
Reduced segregation and a single-phase-like structure will improve oxidation/corrosion resistance and mechanical strength relative to conventionally sintered material.
Standard vacuum sintering of the same Mg-transition-metal blend at 800–1000 °C produces less than 90% relative density.
Standard vacuum sintering at 800–1000 °C causes Mg depletion, transition-metal clustering, and Laves or oxide secondary phases because of incomplete diffusion and thermodynamic instability.
Below 800 °C, insufficient diffusion causes porosity above 10%.
Above 1000 °C, or for dwell times longer than 10 minutes, Mg evaporation causes compositional drift and microstructural instability.
Very-high-melting transition metals such as W or Ta may remain incompletely homogenized at 900 °C even after mechanical alloying.
